Runs can differ in any input, not only covariates: a different phenotype file (another normalization, another sample set), another genotype set, or another reference. Compare them in exactly the same way. Two examples:

A different phenotype file. To see how much power half the samples would give, make a phenotype file with the first 364 samples and run the all-covariate setup on it:

mkdir -p results
gzip -dc examples/mage/data/pheno/mage_expr.chr21_22.regenie.tsv.gz | head -n 365 \
    | gzip > results/expr.half364.regenie.tsv.gz

anqchor cis run \
    --geno-list examples/mage/data/geno/mage.pgen_list.tsv \
    --pheno results/expr.half364.regenie.tsv.gz \
    --pairs examples/mage/data/reference/gtex_lcl_eqtl.chr21_22.tsv.gz \
    --cov examples/mage/data/pheno/mage_covariates.regenie.tsv.gz \
    --out results/cis/peer60_half

anqchor cis compare results/cis/peer60 results/cis/peer60_half \
    --label all729 --label half364 --out results/cis/compare_half

runs.tsv shows n_pheno_samples 729 and 364. At strict, 251 pairs replicate with all samples and 205 with half; at Bonferroni 269 and 225. The same pairs were tested, so no warning is given.

A different reference. Here a third run uses only the 258 reference pairs on chr22, with all covariates:

gzip -dc examples/mage/data/reference/gtex_lcl_eqtl.chr21_22.tsv.gz \
    | awk 'NR == 1 || $2 ~ /^22:/' | gzip > results/ref.chr22.tsv.gz

anqchor cis run \
    --geno-list examples/mage/data/geno/mage.pgen_list.tsv \
    --pheno examples/mage/data/pheno/mage_expr.chr21_22.regenie.tsv.gz \
    --pairs results/ref.chr22.tsv.gz \
    --cov examples/mage/data/pheno/mage_covariates.regenie.tsv.gz \
    --out results/cis/peer60_chr22ref

anqchor cis compare results/cis/peer10 results/cis/peer60 results/cis/peer60_chr22ref \
    --out results/cis/compare_ref

warning: the runs used different reference pairs; compare the common-pair columns (n_rep_<level>_common), which count only pairs tested in every run
warning: the runs tested different pairs: 258 pairs were tested in every run (up to 367 in one run); the *_common columns compare those only
Run n_tested n_rep_strict n_common_tested n_rep_bonferroni_common n_rep_strict_common peer10 367 231 258 180 168 peer60 367 251 258 197 185 peer60_chr22ref 258 185 258 197 185

The plain counts (231, 251, 185) are over different pairs and cannot be compared with each other. The _common columns count the same 258 pairs in every run, so 168 vs 185 is a fair comparison. When the warning appears, compare the _common columns. The recommendation and the report's charts use each run's own counts.

docs.title: Reproduce a run
docs.text:
Every run directory has anqchor.resolved.yaml, and every comparison has a copy of it per run in settings/<label>.anqchor.yaml. Either reproduces the run exactly:

anqchor cis run --config results/cis/compare/settings/peer10.anqchor.yaml \
    --out results/cis/peer10_again

The tables of results/cis/peer10_again are identical to those of results/cis/peer10, except that their rows are labelled with the new directory name. run.json in each run directory records the anqchor version, the qpgen binary with its git commit and checksum, the commands and the host.

The repository also has a hand-written configuration file for the all-covariate run, examples/mage/cis.yaml:

# anqchor cis: replication of known cis-eQTLs for ONE set of inputs.
#
# Each cis run evaluates one set of inputs (genotypes, phenotypes, covariates, phenotype
# transform, reference).
# To compare analysis setups, run 'anqchor cis run' once per setup (into separate
# directories; the runs are independent and can run in parallel) and compare them with
# 'anqchor cis compare RUN_DIR... --out DIR'.
#
# This file is the all-covariate run of the MAGE example (chr21/22 compact data in data/).
# It is equivalent to the flags-only command
#
#   anqchor cis run --geno-list examples/mage/data/geno/mage.pgen_list.tsv \
#       --pheno examples/mage/data/pheno/mage_expr.chr21_22.regenie.tsv.gz \
#       --cov examples/mage/data/pheno/mage_covariates.regenie.tsv.gz \
#       --pairs examples/mage/data/reference/gtex_lcl_eqtl.chr21_22.tsv.gz \
#       --out results/cis/peer60
#
# except for the dataset and reference names (rnaseq and gtex_lcl here, dataset and
# reference with flags). Paths are relative to this file. From the repository root:
#
#   anqchor cis run --config examples/mage/cis.yaml --out results/cis_config
#
version: 1
project: mage_cis
out_dir: ../../results/cis_config      # overridden by --out

genotypes:
  # qpgen pgen list (CHROM BEG END PREFIX): 729 individuals, 256,645 variants (MAF >= 5%).
  pgen_list: data/geno/mage.pgen_list.tsv

references:
  gtex_lcl:
    kind: cis
    # 367 GTEx v10 LCL eGenes on chr21/22 with their sentinel variant (columns trait variant
    # beta se pval), from donors independent of MAGE.
    pairs: data/reference/gtex_lcl_eqtl.chr21_22.tsv.gz
    columns: {trait: trait, variant: variant, beta: beta, se: se, pval: pval}

datasets:
  rnaseq:
    omics: rnaseq
    # 729 samples x 367 genes, regenie layout (FID IID gene...), IDs 'ENSG...:GENE'.
    pheno: data/pheno/mage_expr.chr21_22.regenie.tsv.gz
    pheno_format: regenie
    # Gene TSS loci (BED, same IDs). Not needed by the default pair engine; the rect engine
    # uses them to split its local controls into same- and cross-chromosome cells.
    trait_annot: data/pheno/mage_genes.chr21_22.bed
    # sex (XX/XY, categorical: passed to qpgen as text), PC1-5, PEER1-60: 66 covariates.
    cov: data/pheno/mage_covariates.regenie.tsv.gz
    cov_format: regenie
    trait_id_rule: as_is               # reference and expression trait IDs are identical

pipelines:
  match: {enabled: false}              # this file is for the cis analysis only
  trans: {enabled: false}
  cis:
    reference: gtex_lcl
    assoc_engine: pair                 # pair (pair-assoc) | rect (rect-assoc over variants x traits)
    # One strategy = this run's covariates. 'cov: default' uses every column of the
    # dataset's cov file (same as omitting --cov-include). For a subset, write e.g.
    #   cov: {include: [sex, PC1-5, PEER1-10]}      (= --cov-include sex,PC1-5,PEER1-10)
    # and for no covariates 'cov: null' (= omitting --cov).
    strategies:
      - {name: default, cov: default}
    # Phenotype transform of this run: false = the expression as given; true = rank-based
    # inverse normal transform after covariate adjustment (= --rint). One transform per run.
    rint: false
    levels: {nominal: 0.05, fdr: 0.05, bonferroni: true, strict: 1.0e-5}
    max_unresolved_fraction: 0.2

anqchor cis run --config examples/mage/cis.yaml --out results/cis/peer60_config

It gives the same counts as the flag-only peer60 run; only the dataset and reference names differ (rnaseq and gtex_lcl).

docs.title: The rect engine and local controls
docs.text:
--assoc-engine rect tests the full rectangle of reference variants × reference genes (346 × 367 = 126,982 tests) with qpgen rect-assoc. The 367 reference cells give the replication counts; the other 126,615 cells are kept as local controls. Add the gene positions so that the controls can be split by chromosome:

anqchor cis run \
    --geno-list examples/mage/data/geno/mage.pgen_list.tsv \
    --pheno examples/mage/data/pheno/mage_expr.chr21_22.regenie.tsv.gz \
    --pairs examples/mage/data/reference/gtex_lcl_eqtl.chr21_22.tsv.gz \
    --trait-annot examples/mage/data/pheno/mage_genes.chr21_22.bed \
    --assoc-engine rect \
    --out results/cis_rect/nocov

and likewise for the other setups (about 9 seconds each, in parallel). The replication counts are identical to the pair engine at every level, for every run (β and p agree for every pair). strategies.tsv gains control columns, also shown in a Local controls section of the report:

Run λ_GC, all controls p < 1e-5, all λ_GC, cross-chromosome p < 1e-5, cross-chromosome nocov 1.81 1,367 1.74 445 basic 1.04 157 1.02 1 peer10 1.02 263 1.00 1 peer60 1.02 310 1.00 0 peer60_rint 1.02 311 1.00 0

There are 53,508 cross-chromosome cells. Same-chromosome controls include variants near other real eQTLs (linkage disequilibrium), so they are not a null, and their p < 1e-5 count grows with power. Cross-chromosome cells are much closer to a null: λ_GC ≈ 1 and about half a cell at p < 1e-5 (1e-5 × 53,508) are expected. Every setup with PCs is well calibrated; nocov is not. Without --trait-annot, the cross-chromosome columns are 0 or empty.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Add a setup: for example 30 PEER factors (--cov-include sex,PC1-5,PEER1-30) into results/cis/peer30, then rerun cis compare with six run directories. The existing runs are not touched.
  • Your own normalization: run the same covariates on two phenotype files (for example TMM + inverse normal vs. log CPM), or once as given and once with --rint, and compare them.
  • A subset of runs: cis compare takes any runs in any order; the first is the baseline.
  • A single run's report: anqchor cis report --out results/cis/peer10.

docs.title: Common errors
docs.text:
A covariate name that does not exist. --cov-include names must match the covariate header exactly (case-sensitive), and ranges must stay within the columns:

error in step cis.dataset.default.inputs: unknown covariate name(s) 'Sex'; available: sex, PC1-5, PEER1-60
error: run failed in step cis.dataset.default.inputs; log: results/cis/err/logs/cis.dataset.default.inputs.log

--cov-include without --cov.

error: strategy default: cov.include needs covariates in dataset dataset

--label count does not match the runs. Give one --label per run directory:

error: 1 --label value(s) for 2 run(s)

Not a run directory. cis compare needs directories written by anqchor cis run:

error: results/foo is not an anqchor run directory (no anqchor.resolved.yaml)

Too many unresolved pairs. If more than 20% of the reference pairs cannot be tested, the summary step fails and names examples of absent variants. The usual causes are a different genome build (hg19 vs hg38), chr21 vs 21, swapped REF/ALT, or a different indel representation. Fix the reference rather than raising max_unresolved_fraction.

Trait IDs do not match. If the reference uses ENSG00000015475 and the expression uses ENSG00000015475.19:BID, set --trait-id-rule (for example before_colon_strip_version) or provide a trait map (Inputs).

Two setups in one directory. Each setup needs its own --out. Rerunning into the same directory with other flags replaces that run's tables (an existing report/cis.html there is not updated until you run anqchor cis report again). Two commands cannot run in the same directory at the same time; the second stops with another anqchor command is running in ....

docs.title: Example data
docs.text: The repository ships a compact copy of a real xQTL dataset in examples/mage/data/ (32 MB). Every example in this documentation uses it, so you can run each command as written right after installation.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
• Expression: RNA-seq of lymphoblastoid cell lines (LCLs) from the MAGE study (Multi-ancestry Analysis of Gene Expression), 729 individuals of the 1000 Genomes Project, normalised (TMM, then inverse normal transform per gene).
  • Genotypes: the New York Genome Center (NYGC) high-coverage whole-genome sequencing of the 1000 Genomes samples.
  • Reference: cis-eQTLs from an independent study, GTEx v10: for each gene with a significant eQTL (an eGene) in EBV-transformed lymphocytes, its sentinel (strongest) variant. GTEx donors are not MAGE individuals.
  • Region: chromosomes 21 and 22 only.
What Size Individuals (genotypes and expression) 729 Genotyped variants (MAF ≥ 5%) 256,645 (127,563 on chr21, 129,082 on chr22) Genes (expression and loci) 367 Covariates 66: sex, PC1-5, PEER1-60 Known cis-eQTL pairs 367 (one per gene; 346 distinct variants)

Why the reference comes from another study

The known eQTLs were discovered in GTEx donors, not in these 729 individuals. That makes the comparisons meaningful: a reference discovered in the same samples would fit their own noise, make identity matches look stronger than they are and favour the covariate setup used for its discovery. Use an independent reference with your own data too.

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
examples/mage/data/
├── geno/
│   ├── mage.pgen_list.tsv            pgen list: which file holds which chromosome
│   ├── mage_chr21.pgen               genotypes, chr21 (14.6 MB)
│   ├── mage_chr21.psam               sample IDs
│   ├── mage_chr21.pvar.idx.gz        indexed variant list (1.3 MB)
│   ├── mage_chr21.pvar.idx.gz.tbi    tabix index of the variant list
│   └── mage_chr22.*                  the same for chr22 (15.2 MB pgen)
├── pheno/
│   ├── mage_expr.chr21_22.regenie.tsv.gz      expression, 729 × 367 (0.6 MB)
│   ├── mage_covariates.regenie.tsv.gz         covariates, 729 × 66 (0.2 MB)
│   └── mage_genes.chr21_22.bed                gene TSS loci (17 KB)
└── reference/
    └── gtex_lcl_eqtl.chr21_22.tsv.gz          known cis-eQTL pairs from GTEx (12 KB)

docs.title: Genotypes
docs.text:
The pgen list tells qpgen which PLINK 2 file set holds which chromosome. Columns are chromosome, first position, last position and the file prefix (relative prefixes are looked up next to the list):

$ cat examples/mage/data/geno/mage.pgen_list.tsv
21  1   1000000000  mage_chr21
22  1   1000000000  mage_chr22

The psam lists the samples, one ID per line:

$ head -4 examples/mage/data/geno/mage_chr21.psam
#IID
HG00096
HG00100
HG00105

The indexed pvar (.pvar.idx.gz with its .tbi) lists the variants with an INDEX column giving each variant's row in the .pgen. qpgen looks variants up through the tabix index instead of reading the whole list. anqchor prepare index-pvar makes one from an ordinary .pvar.

$ gzip -dc examples/mage/data/geno/mage_chr21.pvar.idx.gz | head -5
#CHROM  POS ID  REF ALT QUAL    FILTER  INFO    INDEX
21  5031747 21:5031747:G:GA G   GA  .   .   .   1
21  5031747 21:5031748:GA:G GA  G   .   .   .   2
21  5083315 21:5083315:A:C  A   C   .   .   .   3
21  5083679 21:5083679:G:A  G   A   .   .   .   4

The .pgen files are binary. The genotypes are unphased hard calls.

docs.title: Expression
docs.text:
A samples × genes matrix in regenie layout: FID, IID, then one column per gene. Gene IDs are ENSEMBL_ID:GENE_NAME.

$ gzip -dc examples/mage/data/pheno/mage_expr.chr21_22.regenie.tsv.gz | head -3 | cut -f1-5
FID IID ENSG00000275993.3:SIK1B ENSG00000278931.1:bP-2189O9.2   ENSG00000279720.1:SOWAHCP2
HG00096 HG00096 -0.238523   0.224454    2.54496
HG00100 HG00100 -0.217436   -0.309645   -0.0685407

The sample IDs are the genotype IDs, so no sample map is needed.

docs.title: Covariates
docs.text:
The same layout, one column per covariate. sex is text (XX/XY), so it is a categorical covariate: anqchor keeps the text levels and passes --cat-cov-names sex to qpgen, which replaces it by one indicator column (XX is the reference level).

$ gzip -dc examples/mage/data/pheno/mage_covariates.regenie.tsv.gz | head -3 | cut -f1-9
FID IID sex PC1 PC2 PC3 PC4 PC5 PEER1
HG00096 HG00096 XY  -0.0216243  0.0487524   0.00362148  0.0446186   0.00187148  -0.0565679
HG00100 HG00100 XX  -0.0215191  0.0503942   0.00281614  0.040869    0.000118772 0.0722641

The columns after PEER1 are PEER2 to PEER60. With --cov-include you can use a subset, for example --cov-include sex,PC1-5,PEER1-10 (ranges expand).

Non-numeric columns are categorical automatically. A covariate whose categories are coded as numbers, for example a sequencing batch 1, 2, 3, would be read as one numeric covariate; name it with --cat-cov-names batch (config cov_categorical: [batch]) to treat it as categorical. See covariates.

docs.title: Gene loci
docs.text:
A BED-like file with each gene's transcription start site. Gene IDs are the same as in the expression file. trans evaluation uses it to tell cis cells from trans cells; cis evaluation needs it only with --assoc-engine rect.

$ head -4 examples/mage/data/pheno/mage_genes.chr21_22.bed
#chrom  start   end id
21  6111130 6111131 ENSG00000275993.3:SIK1B
21  8857259 8857260 ENSG00000278931.1:bP-2189O9.2
21  9083100 9083101 ENSG00000279720.1:SOWAHCP2

docs.title: Reference pairs
docs.text:
The known cis-eQTLs: trait, variant (CHROM:POS:REF:ALT), effect size, its standard error and p-value. Each row is one GTEx eGene with its sentinel variant; beta, se and pval are GTEx's slope, slope_se and pval_nominal, and beta is the effect of one copy of the ALT allele. The trait is the gene's ID in the expression file (matched on the Ensembl ID without its version).

$ gzip -dc examples/mage/data/reference/gtex_lcl_eqtl.chr21_22.tsv.gz | head -4
trait   variant beta    se  pval
ENSG00000275993.3:SIK1B 21:6122794:C:T  -0.448959   0.0888711   8.054e-07
ENSG00000278931.1:bP-2189O9.2   21:9370164:G:A  0.484109    0.10423 5.31901e-06
ENSG00000279720.1:SOWAHCP2  21:9088050:G:A  0.708996    0.180329    0.000107185

Every reference variant is present in the genotypes, so all 367 pairs are tested. The GTEx p-values range from 1e-102 to 1e-4 (median 8e-11): some eGenes are strong, others barely significant in GTEx, as in any real reference.

docs.title: What the example shows
docs.text:
• Identity matching: 727 of 729 samples are confirmed (14 only leniently). The expression sample labelled NA11919 does not match its own genotypes (rank 253 of 729), and no other individual matches it clearly either, so the result is "unclear" rather than a named mismatch. Both NA11919 and its best (but weak) candidate, HG00237, are in the data (genotypes and expression), so you can inspect the case yourself (identity matching).
  • cis evaluation: the known pairs replicate much better with PEER factors: 178 of 367 at p < 10⁻⁵ without covariates, 251 with all 66 covariates (cis evaluation).

docs.title: How it was made
docs.text:
examples/mage/make_compact_data.sh rebuilds examples/mage/data/ from the full MAGE and NYGC files and the GTEx v10 eGene table for EBV-transformed lymphocytes (Cells_EBV-transformed_lymphocytes.v10.eGenes.txt.gz, part of the single-tissue cis-eQTL data on the GTEx portal). It needs plink2, anqchor and Python with pandas:

bash examples/mage/make_compact_data.sh FULL_DATA_DIR GTEX_EGENES [PLINK2]

FULL_DATA_DIR holds the MAGE and NYGC files, GTEX_EGENES is the path of the GTEx eGene table and PLINK2 the plink2 binary (default: plink2 on your PATH). For example:

bash examples/mage/make_compact_data.sh /data/mage \
    /data/gtex/Cells_EBV-transformed_lymphocytes.v10.eGenes.txt.gz

What it keeps, and why:

Part Kept Why Genotypes the 729 individuals with expression; every variant with MAF ≥ 5% among them; unphased; psam with #IID only; pvar reduced to CHROM POS ID REF ALT, then indexed any common variant can be queried, not just the reference variants, so trans rectangles and your own variant lists work Reference the GTEx eGenes on chr21/22 with q ≤ 0.05 whose sentinel variant is in those genotypes (same CHROM:POS:REF:ALT) and whose gene is in the MAGE expression data (same Ensembl ID, ignoring the version); columns trait variant beta se pval an independent reference in the same cell type, and every pair can be tested Expression the 729 samples × the genes of those reference pairs; values rounded to 6 significant digits the analyses only use genes with a known pair Gene loci the TSS of those genes, with the expression IDs and the genotypes' chromosome names (21, not chr21) IDs and chromosomes match the other files without any mapping Covariates sex, PC1-5, PEER1-60 for the 729 samples, regenie layout, 6 significant digits the covariates used by the MAGE study

Unused columns (the other columns of the GTEx table; the extra pvar columns) are dropped.

Provenance of the full files

The script starts from the NYGC phased chr21/22 genotypes of 3,202 1000 Genomes samples, the MAGE expression matrix of 729 samples × 20,154 genes with its tensorQTL BED, the MAGE covariate table (one row per covariate) and the GTEx v10 eGene table of EBV-transformed lymphocytes. GTEx tests 913 genes on chr21/22 and calls 516 of them eGenes at q ≤ 0.05. Of those 516, 367 are kept: 72 genes are not in the MAGE expression data, 67 have a sentinel variant with MAF below 5% in the 729 individuals, and 10 have a sentinel variant that the genotype release does not contain under the same CHROM:POS:REF:ALT.

docs.title: Use case: is every expression sample paired with the right genotype?
docs.text:
This page checks sample identity in the MAGE example from start to finish. You need about ten minutes. Each command takes a few seconds.

In short

anqchor match run \
  --geno-list examples/mage/data/geno/mage.pgen_list.tsv \
  --pheno     examples/mage/data/pheno/mage_expr.chr21_22.regenie.tsv.gz \
  --cov       examples/mage/data/pheno/mage_covariates.regenie.tsv.gz \
  --pairs     examples/mage/data/reference/gtex_lcl_eqtl.chr21_22.tsv.gz \
  --out results/match
anqchor match report --out results/match
Then open results/match/report/match.html. On this data 713 of the 729 expression samples match their own genotype best and 14 match it only leniently. Two samples are unclear. One of them, NA11919, clearly does not match its own genotype (rank 253 of 729), but no other individual stands out clearly enough to name the source.

docs.title: The question
docs.text:
In an xQTL study, every omics sample (here, an RNA-seq library) is linked to a genotyped individual by its sample ID. Tubes get swapped, libraries get contaminated and spreadsheets get sorted wrongly. If a link is wrong, that sample's genotypes and expression do not belong together. This weakens every association and can create false ones.

Why genetics can answer this. Many genes have strong known cis-eQTLs, where one variant changes the gene's expression by a known amount (beta). If you know an individual's genotypes, you can predict whether each of these genes should be expressed higher or lower than average in that individual. The predicted value is the sum of beta × dosage. This is a polygenic score (PRS) per gene, although here it usually has one variant per gene. Across hundreds of genes these predictions form a profile that fits only one person.

flowchart TB
  A["PRS profile of every<br/>genotyped individual"] --> C
  B["Measured expression<br/>of each sample"] --> C
  C["Correlate and<br/>convert to Z-scores"] --> D{"Is the labelled<br/>individual the best?"}
  D -->|yes| P["PASS"]
  D -->|"close second"| W["WARN"]
  D -->|"another clearly ahead"| F["FAIL"]

anqchor:

  1. computes the PRS profile of every genotyped individual (qpgentools pair-prs);
  2. correlates each expression sample's measured profile with every individual's predicted profile and converts the correlations into Z-scores (qpgentools match-prs-pheno);
  3. checks whether the individual the sample is labelled with has the highest Z. If another individual is clearly ahead, the sample is a mismatch.

A single gene says almost nothing, but 367 genes together identify individuals reliably. On this data, a correctly labelled sample's own genotype typically has Z ≈ 5.5, while the best unrelated individual reaches Z ≈ 3.

The known eQTLs come from GTEx (EBV-transformed lymphocytes), whose donors are not in MAGE. An independent reference matters: eQTLs discovered in the same samples would fit those samples' own expression noise and make every match look stronger than it really is.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
All files are in the repository under examples/mage/data/. The example data page describes where they come from.

File What it is Size geno/mage.pgen_list.tsv list of PLINK2 genotype files, one per chromosome 729 individuals × 256,645 variants geno/mage_chr21.*, geno/mage_chr22.* .pgen, .psam, indexed .pvar.idx.gz (+ .tbi) reference/gtex_lcl_eqtl.chr21_22.tsv.gz known cis-eQTLs from GTEx (the reference) 367 gene–variant pairs, 346 variants pheno/mage_expr.chr21_22.regenie.tsv.gz expression (the omics data to check) 729 samples × 367 genes pheno/mage_covariates.regenie.tsv.gz covariates removed from the expression first 729 samples × 66 covariates

Genotype list (CHROM BEG END PREFIX, no header). Relative prefixes are resolved next to the list file:

21  1   1000000000  mage_chr21
22  1   1000000000  mage_chr22

The .psam has only an #IID column:

#IID
HG00096
HG00100

The indexed .pvar.idx.gz holds CHROM POS ID REF ALT plus the row number of each variant in the .pgen (INDEX):

#CHROM  POS      ID               REF  ALT  QUAL  FILTER  INFO  INDEX
21      5031747  21:5031747:G:GA  G    GA   .     .       .     1
21      5031747  21:5031748:GA:G  GA   G    .     .       .     2

The genotypes are the 729 individuals that have expression data, with every variant of minor allele frequency ≥ 5% among them. They are unphased.

Reference pairs (tab-separated with a header; pval is optional). One row per GTEx eGene: the gene and its sentinel (strongest) variant. Variant IDs are CHROM:POS:REF:ALT. beta is the effect of one copy of ALT on the gene's expression:

trait                          variant         beta       se         pval
ENSG00000275993.3:SIK1B        21:6122794:C:T  -0.448959  0.0888711  8.054e-07
ENSG00000278931.1:bP-2189O9.2  21:9370164:G:A  0.484109   0.10423    5.31901e-06
ENSG00000279720.1:SOWAHCP2     21:9088050:G:A  0.708996   0.180329   0.000107185

Expression, in regenie layout: one row per sample with FID, IID, then one column per gene. The gene IDs are identical to the reference trait IDs. The sample IDs (IID) are identical to the genotype IDs, so no sample map is needed:

FID      IID      ENSG00000275993.3:SIK1B  ENSG00000278931.1:bP-2189O9.2  ENSG00000279720.1:SOWAHCP2  ...
HG00096  HG00096  -0.238523                0.224454                       2.54496                     ...
HG00100  HG00100  -0.217436                -0.309645                      -0.0685407                  ...

Covariates, also in regenie layout: sex, PC1–PC5, PEER1–PEER60. sex is text (XX/XY). anqchor detects that it is not numeric and passes it to qpgen as a categorical covariate (--cat-cov-names sex), which qpgen encodes as an indicator column. Categories coded as numbers, such as a batch number, need --cat-cov-names batch:

FID      IID      sex  PC1         PC2        ...  PEER1       ...  PEER60
HG00096  HG00096  XY   -0.0216243  0.0487524  ...  -0.0565679  ...  ...
HG00100  HG00100  XX   -0.0215191  0.0503942  ...  0.0722641   ...  ...

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
From the repository root:

anqchor match run \
  --geno-list examples/mage/data/geno/mage.pgen_list.tsv \
  --pheno     examples/mage/data/pheno/mage_expr.chr21_22.regenie.tsv.gz \
  --cov       examples/mage/data/pheno/mage_covariates.regenie.tsv.gz \
  --pairs     examples/mage/data/reference/gtex_lcl_eqtl.chr21_22.tsv.gz \
  --out results/match

[anqchor] running prepare.genotypes
[anqchor] running prepare.reference.reference
[anqchor] running prepare.dataset.dataset
[anqchor] running prepare.mapping.dataset.reference
[anqchor] running prs.reference
[anqchor] running match.dataset.qpgen
[anqchor] running match.dataset.summarize
ran: prepare.genotypes, prepare.reference.reference, ..., match.dataset.qpgen, match.dataset.summarize

This takes about 8 seconds on a laptop. match run stops at the summary tables. Render the HTML report from them (about 1 second, no analysis is run):

anqchor match report --out results/match

match report: results/match/report/match.html

anqchor match all with the same flags does both in one command. Running match run again with the same flags does nothing (ran: nothing (all steps up to date)).

What the flags mean:

  • --geno-list is the genotype list. With a single PLINK2 fileset, use --pfile path/prefix instead.
  • --pheno is the omics matrix to check.
  • --cov holds covariates that are regressed out of the expression before matching. This removes sex, ancestry and hidden technical factors, so the remaining variation is driven more by the eQTL genotypes (see its effect).
  • --pairs is the reference: known xQTL effects.
  • --out is the run directory.

The defaults that apply: rank-based inverse normal transform after the covariate adjustment (--rint), genes scored as independent (--independent), --z-threshold 1.96, --z-diff 2. With flag-only inputs the dataset and reference are called dataset and reference, which appear in step names and output paths; --dataset-name rnaseq --reference-name gtex_lcl changes them. Other flags you may need with your own data: --sample-map when omics and genotype IDs differ (example below), --trait-id-rule when gene IDs differ (such as with or without the version), and --prs-samples to restrict the candidate individuals.

The same run from a configuration file

examples/mage/match.yaml describes the same inputs and settings, with comments:

anqchor match run --config examples/mage/match.yaml --out results/match_cfg

It names the dataset rnaseq and the reference gtex_lcl, so its outputs are under match/rnaseq/. The calls are identical. Every run directory also holds anqchor.resolved.yaml, the complete settings of that run (flags included); anqchor match run --config results/match/anqchor.resolved.yaml --out results/match_again repeats it exactly.

docs.title: What comes out
docs.text:
results/match/
├── match/dataset/
│   ├── summary.json           counts, verdict, failing samples, parameters
│   ├── samples.tsv            one row per expression sample
│   ├── swaps.tsv              reciprocal swaps and one-way mismatches
│   ├── candidates.tsv         rescue candidates (unlabelled samples with a clear match)
│   ├── duplicates.tsv         samples that match two genotype IDs about equally
│   ├── related.tsv            samples whose top matches include possible relatives
│   ├── weights.tsv            per-gene weight (how informative each gene is)
│   └── qpgen.*                qpgen's own outputs and the exact command line
├── prs/reference/             predicted expression (PRS) of every genotyped individual
├── prepare/                   normalised inputs; prepare/references/reference/reference.json
│                              reports 346 of 346 reference variants present
├── report/match.html          written by 'match report' (or 'match all')
├── logs/<step>.log            one log per step
├── anqchor.resolved.yaml      the complete settings of the run
└── run.json                   command lines, qpgen binary and commit, step times

docs.title: summary.json
docs.text:
The first lines to read:

"group_counts":  {"FAIL": 0, "NO_TEST": 0, "PASS": 713, "WARN": 16},
"status_counts": {"SELF_BEST": 713, "SELF_LENIENT": 14, "UNCLEAR": 2, ...},
"verdict": "727 of 729 mapped samples confirmed (14 only leniently); 2 unclear",
"verdict_status": "warning",
"n_traits_used": 367, "n_traits_weight_le0": 14, "n_prs_samples": 729,
"n_reciprocal_swaps": 0, "n_rescue_candidates": 0, "n_duplicates": 0, "n_related": 8
  • verdict is the one-sentence result. verdict_status is critical whenever at least one sample fails, warning when some are unclear, good otherwise.
  • group_counts sums the statuses into four groups: PASS (own genotype is the best), WARN (own genotype is not the best, but nobody else is clearly ahead), FAIL (someone else is clearly ahead), NO_TEST (nothing to check, for example no label).
  • failing lists each FAIL with its Z-scores and note.
  • weights summarises how informative the genes are (the correlation of each gene's PRS with its measured expression). Here the median weight is 0.24 and 14 of the 367 genes have a weight ≤ 0. For 13 of them the GTEx effect does not show up in MAGE (p > 0.001 for the reference variant with all covariates); for one, HMGN1, MAGE shows a strong effect in the opposite direction. Such genes carry no identity information. Many genes with weight ≤ 0 would point to a wrong gene mapping or a reference that does not fit the data (another tissue, wrong allele coding).

docs.title: swaps.tsv
docs.text: Every FAIL sample appears here. Two samples whose best matches are each other's labels are a reciprocal pair; any other FAIL is one-way, with the sample that holds its best genotype as partner. The file is empty here because no sample fails. A real swap of two samples appears as two rows of kind reciprocal (see below).

docs.title: candidates.tsv
docs.text: Rescue candidates are expression samples without a genotype label that clearly match a genotyped individual (candidate_geno_id). The file is empty here because every sample is labelled. With your own data, unlabelled samples appear here when the sample map leaves them out (example below). A sample whose clear best genotype is already the confirmed match of another sample is not a candidate.

docs.title: duplicates.tsv
docs.text: Samples that match two genotype IDs about equally: the top two score alike (the second at least 0.8 × the first) and both stand clear of every other genotype (rule). The two genotypes are then most likely one person. The file is empty here; below is an example with a duplicated genotype.

docs.title: related.tsv
docs.text:
8 samples have top candidates that start with a block of two or three individuals standing out from the rest. One is usually the sample itself, and another has Z ≈ 3.5–4.8, about what a close relative gives (1000 Genomes contains families). For example:

pheno_id  group  n_close  close_ids                close_z
HG02429   PASS   2        HG02429,HG02479          6.441,4.782
NA12046   WARN   3        HG04141,NA12046,NA19717  3.824,3.607,3.524

This is for information only, does not change any call and is not shown in the report. assigned_in_close says whether the labelled genotype is part of the block. Where the own genotype scores well (Z 5–7.8, six samples), the relative scores 0.51–0.74 of the best, far below the near-equal scores of a duplicated genotype. Where it scores weakly (HG02574 at 4.0, NA12046 at 3.6), the block is close to even; that is weak signal, not evidence of a duplicate.

docs.title: weights.tsv
docs.text: One row per gene: trait, ref_trait (the reference trait it came from), weight, n_obs (samples observed) and weight_le0 (1 when the gene carries no identity information).

docs.title: Reading the report
docs.text:
Open results/match/report/match.html in a browser. It is a single file that works offline. From top to bottom:

  • Header: the title, the counts (729 omics samples · 729 genotypes · 367 traits) and the scoring used. With the default independent scoring a short tip names --mahalanobis.
  • Dashboard: large tiles with the counts, number first. On this data: 729 with an assigned ID, 713 strict matches to their own ID, 727 lenient matches ("strict + 14"), 0 samples that match another sample and 2 whose own ID is too weak (not the top match and at or below the lenient cutoff: NA11919 and NA12717). "Matches two genotype IDs", "Matches several" and "Not scored" tiles appear when such samples exist, and a "No assigned ID" tile when some samples have no ID. Click a tile to filter the sample table. The same result names are used on the tiles, cards, chart legend, filters and table.
  • Sliders: the lenient cutoff (z_threshold) and the clear lead (z_diff), each with a one-line hint, and one line explaining the match score. Moving either reclassifies every sample in your browser with the same rules qpgen uses, and the tiles, cards, chart, duplicates and table follow. A changed tile shows the run's count under its value. Reset returns to the run's values, and Copy as config copies the YAML lines that make new values permanent. The files in the run directory are not changed. Use this to explore the trade-offs below without re-running.
  • Samples to check: one card per sample that is not a strict match, with bars for the own-ID match score and the best other score, and the lenient cutoff as a dashed tick. Here 16 samples: the two whose own ID is too weak come first, then the lenient matches. At most 12 cards are shown, followed by "Show all 16 in table →". The NA11919 card reads "Best: HG00237, ahead of next by 0.32 (needs more than 2.00). HG00237 also matches its own sample." Samples that match two genotype IDs and samples without an assigned ID get cards too; when more than six samples have no ID, one card summarises them. The report calls qpgen's Z-score the "match score".
  • How clearly each sample matches one genotype: one point per sample, assigned or not: best match score across, runner-up score up. Below the dashed line (shaded, "one genotype clearly best") the best genotype leads the runner-up by more than the clear lead; the line moves with the slider (the shade is grey: a mismatch can lie there too). On the dotted diagonal the two tie. Strict matches form the green cloud at best 3–8.4 and runner-up 2.3–4.8. The 14 lenient points sit near the diagonal at 2.2–4.3, and NA11919 sits close to them at (3.6, 3.3): its own genotype is far down the list, but no other genotype clearly fits it either. A sample whose expression came from another genotyped individual would sit in the shaded part instead. Samples without an assigned ID are hollow markers; a duplicated genotype shows as a star on the diagonal far above the cloud.
  • Duplicates: samples that match two genotype IDs about equally. None here ("No sample matches two genotype IDs."). Mismatches and relatives are not listed.
  • All samples: every sample with its result, own score, own rank, best other ID, its score, lead (own score minus the best other score; negative when another genotype fits better, in red when that makes the sample a mismatch) and the suggested ID. For samples without an assigned ID the lead is the best genotype's lead over the next, in italics. The page scrolls and the header stays on screen. On a phone the table keeps sample, result, own score and lead, and shows the best other genotype under the sample ID. Search by ID, filter by result, sort by any column, show 100, 500 (the default) or all rows per page, and download the view as TSV.
  • Run details (collapsed): the settings, a histogram of gene weights (−0.35 to 0.80 here, 14 genes at or below zero), the result names and the matching codes in samples.tsv, the qpgen command line and the qpgen log.

The report uses plain names for the qpgen statuses:

Report samples.tsv qpgen_status Strict match SELF_BEST Lenient match SELF_LENIENT Matches another sample (assigned ID) / New ID found or ID already used (no assigned ID) SINGLE_NEW_BEST Matches several MULTI_NEW_BEST Matches two genotype IDs (about equally, one of them the own ID or no ID assigned) SINGLE_NEW_BEST or MULTI_NEW_BEST Own ID too weak UNCLEAR No clear match (no assigned ID) NO_SELF Not scored NO_OBS_TRAITS, NOT_SCORED

docs.title: What the results mean on this data
docs.text:
NA11919: the expression does not come from NA11919, and its source cannot be named. Its own genotype reaches only Z 0.41 and ranks 253rd of 729, which is background level; a correctly labelled sample typically reaches Z ≈ 5.5. So the label is almost certainly wrong. The best candidate is HG00237 (Z 3.60), and it stays the best with every scoring option on this page (below). But it leads the runner-up (NA18553, Z 3.28) by only 0.32, far below the clear lead of 2, and Z 3.6 is a score that the best unrelated individual often reaches for other samples. qpgen therefore calls the sample UNCLEAR (WARN, "Own ID too weak" in the report) and names no new ID. Moreover, HG00237 has its own expression sample, which matches HG00237 normally (PASS, Z 5.17), so even a clear lead would not lead to a relabel: one individual would get two libraries.

The NA11919 library may come from someone who is not among the 729 genotyped individuals, be a mixture, or be of poor quality. Action: exclude NA11919 from downstream analyses and check the lab records. Do not rename it.

NA12717 is most likely weak signal. Its own genotype ranks 13th (Z 1.94), but every candidate, including the best (NA19404, Z 2.71), is at background level and the best leads by only 0.03. Nothing points to another individual, and with --mahalanobis (own ID 6th, lenient) or without covariates (own ID first) it is confirmed. Keep it, but note it.

The 14 lenient (WARN) samples are weak signal, not errors. Their own genotype is a close second to sixth (Z 2.1–3.9), at most 0.75 behind the best, and none has a clear alternative individual. Their expression carries less eQTL signal on these 367 genes. A larger reference (more genes, or genome-wide eQTLs) would most likely confirm them.

docs.title: When the true source is not genotyped
docs.text:
Matching can only name the individual an expression sample really comes from when that individual's genotypes are among the candidates. Here all 729 individuals with expression data are candidates, yet NA11919 has no clear match: its source may be missing, or the signal may be too weak to name it.

To see how a sample behaves when its candidate disappears, leave HG00237, the best candidate for NA11919, out of the candidates with --prs-samples (a file with the other 728 IDs):

mkdir -p results
grep -v -e '^#' -e '^HG00237$' examples/mage/data/geno/mage_chr21.psam > results/without_HG00237.txt
anqchor match run \
  --geno-list examples/mage/data/geno/mage.pgen_list.tsv \
  --pheno     examples/mage/data/pheno/mage_expr.chr21_22.regenie.tsv.gz \
  --cov       examples/mage/data/pheno/mage_covariates.regenie.tsv.gz \
  --pairs     examples/mage/data/reference/gtex_lcl_eqtl.chr21_22.tsv.gz \
  --prs-samples results/without_HG00237.txt \
  --out results/match_noHG00237

NA11919 stays UNCLEAR (WARN). Its own genotype is still at background level (Z 0.41), and the new best, NA18553 at Z 3.31, leads the next (HG02023, Z 3.23) by only 0.08: no individual stands out. The expression sample HG00237 has no genotype candidate any more and becomes NO_SELF (NO_TEST); its best remaining genotype, NA18626 at Z 3.15, is at background level, as expected when the true source is missing.

With your own data, include every genotyped individual you have, not only those with omics data. This is the default. Extra individuals let anqchor name the source of a mislabelled sample and rescue unlabelled samples, and they make it more likely that relatives are among the candidates. Note that more candidates also raise the background: the best unrelated individual scores higher when there are more of them to choose from. A borderline call can then change. For example, a mismatch whose gap is just above z_diff with the 729 candidates here could fall just below it with a larger genotype set and become UNCLEAR instead of FAIL, or the reverse. Calls with a large gap do not change.

docs.title: How the thresholds change the calls
docs.text:
z_threshold and z_diff only decide what happens to samples whose own genotype is not the best. SELF_BEST (PASS) does not depend on them. To see the effect, re-run match run into the same output directory with new values:

anqchor match run \
  --geno-list examples/mage/data/geno/mage.pgen_list.tsv \
  --pheno     examples/mage/data/pheno/mage_expr.chr21_22.regenie.tsv.gz \
  --cov       examples/mage/data/pheno/mage_covariates.regenie.tsv.gz \
  --pairs     examples/mage/data/reference/gtex_lcl_eqtl.chr21_22.tsv.gz \
  --z-threshold 3 --z-diff 1 \
  --out results/match

[anqchor] running match.dataset.qpgen
[anqchor] running match.dataset.summarize
ran: match.dataset.qpgen, match.dataset.summarize
match report: results/match/report/match.html is older than the results; update it with 'anqchor match report --out results/match'

Only the matching and summary steps re-run; the prepared inputs and the PRS are reused. The report is not updated by match run, as the last line says: run anqchor match report --out results/match again to see the new values in it. Results on this data:

The columns use the report's names (qpgen_status in brackets); duplicates.tsv and related.tsv are the numbers of samples listed there.

z_threshold z_diff Strict match (SELF_BEST) Lenient only (SELF_LENIENT) Matches another sample (SINGLE_NEW_BEST) Two genotype IDs or matches several (MULTI_NEW_BEST) Own ID too weak (UNCLEAR) duplicates.tsv related.tsv 1.96 1 713 13 0 1 2 1 7 1.96 2 713 14 0 0 2 0 8 (default) 1.96 3 713 14 0 0 2 0 8 3 1 713 6 0 1 9 1 7 3 2 713 7 0 0 9 0 8 3 3 713 7 0 0 9 0 8 5 1 713 0 0 1 15 0 0 5 2 713 0 0 0 16 0 0 5 3 713 0 0 0 16 0 0

How to read it:

  • z_diff controls how easily a sample fails. No sample has a best match more than 0.76 ahead of the runner-up unless it is its own genotype, so at z_diff 2 and 3 nothing fails. At z_diff 1, two samples are flagged, and both are false alarms. NA12046 becomes MULTI_NEW_BEST ("Matches several", a FAIL): its top three, HG04141 (3.82), itself (3.61) and NA19717 (3.52), are more than 1 ahead of the fourth (2.38). HG02574 stays a strict match but is listed in duplicates.tsv: it scores 4.00 and HG03091 3.81, both more than 1 ahead of the third (2.76). All these scores are at the level of weak true matches. A small z_diff flags more and catches subtle problems, but also produces false alarms. A large one flags only very clear mismatches.
  • z_threshold decides lenient versus unclear. It moves samples between SELF_LENIENT ("own genotype is still good") and UNCLEAR ("cannot tell"), and never changes strict matches or samples that match another sample. At 3, 7 of the 14 lenient samples (own Z 2.1–2.96) become UNCLEAR. At 5, all 14 do. NA11919 and NA12717 are UNCLEAR at every setting. The possible-relatives flag also requires Z ≥ z_threshold, so at 5 no relatives are listed.
  • The default 1.96 / 2 is a sensible start. With few reference genes (weaker Z overall), consider a lower z_diff, then inspect every sample that matches another sample by hand.

The sliders in the report give the same counts instantly, without a re-run.

docs.title: Other scoring options
docs.text:
Each row is the command from Run it with the option added, into a new --out directory (or the same one: only the matching and summary steps re-run):

Option Effect on this data none (covariates, --rint, independent traits) 713 strict, 14 lenient only, 2 own ID too weak (NA11919, NA12717) --mahalanobis better; see Independent vs Mahalanobis scoring --no-rint 714 strict, 13 lenient only, the same 2 own ID too weak (NA11919: own Z 0.40, best HG00237 at 3.83, gap 0.46) --no-use-cov 678 strict, 47 lenient only, 4 own ID too weak. NA11919 stays UNCLEAR (own Z 0.49, best still HG00237 at 3.27, gap 0.52), while NA12717 becomes a strict match. The median gene weight falls from 0.24 to 0.16, and 28 genes instead of 14 get weight ≤ 0.

Removing the covariates (sex, ancestry PCs, PEER factors) matters most. Without the adjustment, shared non-genetic expression variation hides the eQTL signal. Keep the covariate adjustment when you have good covariates. Mahalanobis scoring accounts for correlated genes, for example several eQTL genes in one region; it is slower on large references. --lambda has an effect only together with --mahalanobis; on its own it is accepted and ignored.

docs.title: Independent vs Mahalanobis scoring
docs.text:
By default each trait (here, each gene) is scored independently. --mahalanobis accounts for correlation between traits, with a shrinkage λ chosen automatically (0.58 here; the report shows it under Run details). Run both into separate directories:

anqchor match run \
  --geno-list examples/mage/data/geno/mage.pgen_list.tsv \
  --pheno     examples/mage/data/pheno/mage_expr.chr21_22.regenie.tsv.gz \
  --cov       examples/mage/data/pheno/mage_covariates.regenie.tsv.gz \
  --pairs     examples/mage/data/reference/gtex_lcl_eqtl.chr21_22.tsv.gz \
  --out results/match_indep

anqchor match run \
  --geno-list examples/mage/data/geno/mage.pgen_list.tsv \
  --pheno     examples/mage/data/pheno/mage_expr.chr21_22.regenie.tsv.gz \
  --cov       examples/mage/data/pheno/mage_covariates.regenie.tsv.gz \
  --pairs     examples/mage/data/reference/gtex_lcl_eqtl.chr21_22.tsv.gz \
  --mahalanobis \
  --out results/match_maha
Scoring Strict match Lenient only Own ID too weak Matches another sample Mean own-ID match score (Z) independent traits (default) 713 14 2 0 5.42 --mahalanobis (auto λ 0.58) 724 4 1 0 5.89

Mahalanobis scoring accounts for correlation between traits and matched better on this example: 11 more strict matches, and only NA11919 remains UNCLEAR. Its own genotype is still at background level (Z 0.74, rank 161), and HG00237 is still its best match, now at Z 4.31, but only 0.68 ahead of the runner-up (NA18553, 3.64): still no clear lead.

docs.title: Try it yourself: a sample swap
docs.text:
Make a sample map that swaps the labels of HG00096 and HG00100 and keeps everyone else unchanged. A sample map is a TSV with header geno_id pheno_id. Each row says "expression sample pheno_id is labelled with genotype geno_id":

mkdir -p results
awk 'BEGIN { OFS = "\t"; print "geno_id", "pheno_id" }
     !/^#/ { p = $1
             if (p == "HG00096") p = "HG00100"; else if (p == "HG00100") p = "HG00096"
             print $1, p }' examples/mage/data/geno/mage_chr21.psam > results/swapped_map.tsv
head -3 results/swapped_map.tsv

geno_id pheno_id
HG00096 HG00100
HG00100 HG00096

Run with the map:

anqchor match run \
  --geno-list examples/mage/data/geno/mage.pgen_list.tsv \
  --pheno     examples/mage/data/pheno/mage_expr.chr21_22.regenie.tsv.gz \
  --cov       examples/mage/data/pheno/mage_covariates.regenie.tsv.gz \
  --pairs     examples/mage/data/reference/gtex_lcl_eqtl.chr21_22.tsv.gz \
  --sample-map results/swapped_map.tsv \
  --out results/match_swap
anqchor match report --out results/match_swap

anqchor flags both samples and pairs them as a reciprocal swap (from summary.json):

verdict: 725 of 729 mapped samples confirmed (14 only leniently); 1 mismatch
         (HG00096 (labelled HG00100) best matches HG00096); 3 unclear
group_counts: PASS 711, WARN 17, FAIL 1;  n_reciprocal_swaps: 1

swaps.tsv:

kind        pheno_id  geno_id_assigned  group  best_id  z_best   z_self     rank_self  partner_pheno_id
reciprocal  HG00096   HG00100           FAIL   HG00096  6.23703  0.831925   138        HG00100
reciprocal  HG00100   HG00096           WARN   HG00100  4.65304  -1.05686   627        HG00096

With the wrong labels the own genotypes score at background level or below zero, and each sample's best match is the other label. The two calls differ: HG00096 (labelled HG00100) leads its runner-up by 3.19 and is a mismatch (FAIL) with proposed_geno_id HG00096; HG00100 (labelled HG00096) leads by only 1.76, just below z_diff 2, so it is UNCLEAR (WARN) and gets no proposal. Because one side is a clear mismatch and the best matches point at each other, the pair still counts as a reciprocal swap: relabelling both resolves it. With --z-diff 1.5 both would be FAIL. This is one reason not to set z_diff too high. The Z-scores of other samples move slightly (NA11919's best, HG00237: 3.61 instead of 3.60) because the gene weights are estimated from the mapped samples, which now include two wrong pairs.

After matching

cis and trans do not read the match results and do not accept a sample map. Fix the sample IDs in your input files (or drop the bad samples) before you run them.

docs.title: Try it yourself: samples without an ID
docs.text:
Rename five expression samples (in the expression and covariate files) so that no genotype carries their ID:

mkdir -p results/noid
for f in mage_expr.chr21_22 mage_covariates; do
  zcat < examples/mage/data/pheno/$f.regenie.tsv.gz |
    awk 'BEGIN { FS = OFS = "\t" }
         $2 ~ /^(HG00096|HG02282|HG03127|NA11919|NA12717)$/ { $2 = "_" $2; $1 = $2 } 1' |
    gzip > results/noid/$f.tsv.gz
done
anqchor match all \
  --geno-list examples/mage/data/geno/mage.pgen_list.tsv \
  --pheno     results/noid/mage_expr.chr21_22.tsv.gz \
  --cov       results/noid/mage_covariates.tsv.gz \
  --pairs     examples/mage/data/reference/gtex_lcl_eqtl.chr21_22.tsv.gz \
  --out results/match_noid

The "No assigned ID" tile shows 5: "1 new ID found · 4 no clear match". Each of the five gets a card, and each is a hollow marker in the chart:

Sample Result Best genotype (score) Next (score) _HG00096 New ID found HG00096 (6.23) 3.07 _HG02282 No clear match; "Best: HG02282, ahead of next by 1.19 (needs more than 2.00). No other sample has HG02282." HG02282 (4.21) 3.02 _HG03127 No clear match; "Best: HG03127, ahead of next by 1.08 (needs more than 2.00). No other sample has HG03127." HG03127 (4.46) 3.38 _NA11919 No clear match; "Best: HG00237, ahead of next by 0.31 (needs more than 2.00)." HG00237 (3.60) 3.29 _NA12717 No clear match NA19404 (2.70) 2.69

candidates.tsv lists the one new ID. The best genotypes of _HG02282 and _HG03127 are right, but their leads (1.19 and 1.08) are below the clear lead, so no ID is suggested; that no other sample holds that genotype is weaker evidence, shown only as a note. A sample without an ID whose clear best genotype is already the confirmed match of another sample is shown as "ID already used" instead of "New ID found"; none occurs here.

With many samples without an ID, one summary card replaces the individual cards. Renaming 150 random samples the same way gives "100 new ID found · 50 no clear match": the best genotype is the right one for 148 of the 150, and for 48 of the 50 with no clear match the best genotype isn't used by any other sample, so it is probably theirs (shown as a hint, no ID is suggested). In the table these rows show the best genotype and, in italics, its lead over the next. Fewer labelled samples also change the gene weights a little, so Z-scores near a threshold can move: NA11919 (not renamed) then leads by 0.24 instead of 0.32.

Samples renamed in the expression file only have no covariates: qpgen does not score them (NOT_SCORED, "Not scored"), and the report shows the warning "5 samples not scored: no covariates" and one card listing them.

docs.title: Try it yourself: a genotype listed twice
docs.text:
A person genotyped twice under two IDs (or identical twins) makes an omics sample match two genotype IDs equally well. With HG00096's genotypes copied under a second ID (made with plink2), the expression sample HG00096 scores 6.14 against both, and 2.97 against the next. Its own ID still ranks first, so it stays a strict match, and the report lists it under Duplicates with a card ("HG00096 and HG00096_dup are probably one person").

When the copy differs slightly (the original renamed HG00096_twin, and a copy with 2% of its genotype calls changed at random kept as HG00096), the original scores 6.16 and the own ID 5.55; the exact values depend on which calls change. qpgen calls this MULTI_NEW_BEST, a FAIL; the report shows "Matches two genotype IDs" (with its own tile), not a mismatch. duplicates.tsv has the row; the verdict, n_fail, failing and swaps.tsv leave it out (n_fail_two_ids counts it), and no relabel is proposed. For a sample without an assigned ID matching both copies, the result is "Matches two genotype IDs" too, with no suggested ID.

A weak duplicate is not flagged: copying HG03127, whose own score is only 4.50, gives two equal scores that do not stand clear of the background (third best 3.31). It is listed in related.tsv as a possible relative instead.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Change the thresholds with the report's sliders. Use Copy as config, or re-run match run with --z-threshold / --z-diff, to make them permanent.
  • Try --mahalanobis (--lambda auto) when your reference genes are correlated.
  • Run the identity check on your own data: the same four input flags, plus --sample-map when omics IDs differ from genotype IDs.
  • Once identities are fixed, evaluate your analysis setup with cis evaluation.
  • The full status rules, swap and relative detection and every output column: match pipeline.

docs.title: Use case: trans evaluation
docs.text:
Question. Before you scan for trans-eQTLs (a variant affecting a gene far away), you want to know three things about your analysis setup:

  1. Does it recover the known eQTLs, cis and trans?
  2. Does it report hotspots, regions whose variants seem to affect many genes, and do they survive good covariates?
  3. Are its p-values calibrated: when there is no real effect, do they behave like p-values, or are false positives inflated?

This page runs anqchor trans on the compact MAGE example shipped with the repository, once for each of five setups (no covariates, three covariate sets, and RINT), compares the five runs and walks through the results.

Three commands

  1. anqchor trans run, once per setup: tests one setup and writes its own run directory.
  2. anqchor trans compare RUN_DIR... --out DIR: puts the runs side by side and writes one report.
  3. anqchor trans report --out DIR: re-renders that report later, in about a second.

The trans analysis runs on its own, separately from match and cis.

docs.title: What anqchor tests
docs.text:
anqchor tests a rectangle: every variant of the reference pairs against every gene of the reference pairs. Here the reference is 367 GTEx eQTL pairs with 346 distinct variants, so the rectangle is 346 variants × 367 genes = 126,982 tests ("cells"), each a linear regression of the gene's expression on the variant's genotype.

flowchart TB
  R["346 variants × 367 genes<br/>= 126,982 cells"] --> C["cis: 6,186<br/>(same chromosome, ≤ 1 Mb)"]
  R --> T["trans: 120,796"]
  T --> X["other chromosome: 53,508"]
  T --> D["same chromosome, > 1 Mb: 67,288"]
  C --> P["1. replicated pairs"]
  T --> H["2. hotspots"]
  X --> N["3. inflation"]

cis or trans. A pair is cis when the variant is on the gene's chromosome within 1 Mb (--cis-window-bp) of the gene's start (TSS). Every other pair is trans: on another chromosome, or on the same chromosome more than 1 Mb away. The gene positions come from --trait-annot.

1. Replicated reference pairs. Each reference pair is one cell of the rectangle. It replicates when the effect has the reference's sign, and at stricter levels also p < 0.05 or p < 1e-5. cis and trans pairs are counted separately: trans effects are weaker and much harder to replicate.

2. Hotspots. Only trans cells count. The variants are grouped into 1-Mb bins (--hotspot-bin-bp); a bin's count is the number of different genes with a trans signal (p below a threshold) from any variant in the bin. Genes that are in cis with the bin (start within 1 Mb of one of its variants) are not counted, so the tail of a cis eQTL is never counted as a trans signal. A hotspot is a bin with at least k genes (default 5). Because the right threshold depends on the number of tests, anqchor counts hotspots for every threshold among p < 1e-4, 1e-5, 1e-6, 5e-8, 1e-8, 1e-10 and Bonferroni (0.05 / trans cells = 4.1e-7 here) and every k among 1, 2, 3, 5, 10 and 20.

3. Inflation. A variant on chromosome 21 and a gene on chromosome 22 are, with very few exceptions, unrelated. So the p-values of the cross-chromosome cells should look like draws from a uniform distribution. Three summaries check that:

  • λ_GC (genomic control inflation factor) = median χ²(1) statistic of the cells / 0.4549, the median of a χ²(1) distribution. Calibrated tests give λ_GC ≈ 1; above 1.1 anqchor warns.
  • Observed vs expected cells below p < 1e-3 and p < 1e-5: with 53,508 null cells, 53.5 and 0.5 are expected.
  • The QQ plot: observed against expected −log10 p. Calibrated tests stay inside the grey 95% band around the diagonal.

When the reference has trans pairs, their regions are left out of these cells first (every variant within 1 Mb of a reference trans variant, and every cell of a reference trans gene), so that known trans signals do not look like inflation. The GTEx reference here is cis only, so nothing is left out.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
All inputs are in examples/mage/data/ (see Example data for each file); the commands below run from the repository root.

File What it is Flag geno/mage.pgen_list.tsv + geno/mage_chr21.*, geno/mage_chr22.* genotypes: 729 individuals × 256,645 variants with MAF ≥ 5% --geno-list pheno/mage_expr.chr21_22.regenie.tsv.gz expression, 729 samples × 367 genes (regenie layout) --pheno pheno/mage_genes.chr21_22.bed gene start (TSS) of each gene: 109 on chr21, 258 on chr22 --trait-annot pheno/mage_covariates.regenie.tsv.gz covariates: sex (XX/XY), PC1-PC5, PEER1-PEER60 --cov reference/gtex_lcl_eqtl.chr21_22.tsv.gz 367 GTEx eQTL pairs (346 variants: 106 on chr21, 240 on chr22) --pairs

The gene loci file is BED-like (chrom start end id, IDs as in the expression file):

examples/mage/data/pheno/mage_genes.chr21_22.bed (first lines)
#chrom  start   end id
21  6111130 6111131 ENSG00000275993.3:SIK1B
21  8857259 8857260 ENSG00000278931.1:bP-2189O9.2

The reference has one row per eQTL (trait variant beta se pval, variant CHROM:POS:REF:ALT):

examples/mage/data/reference/gtex_lcl_eqtl.chr21_22.tsv.gz (first lines)
trait                          variant         beta       se         pval
ENSG00000275993.3:SIK1B        21:6122794:C:T  -0.448959  0.0888711  8.054e-07
ENSG00000278931.1:bP-2189O9.2  21:9370164:G:A  0.484109   0.10423    5.31901e-06

These are GTEx v10 eGenes of EBV-transformed lymphocytes (the cell type of MAGE) with their sentinel variant; GTEx donors are not MAGE individuals, so the reference is independent of this data. All 367 pairs are cis. A typical trans reference mixes cis and trans pairs; this one tests only the cis side of item 1, and the report says that there are no trans pairs.

docs.title: Run the five setups
docs.text:
D=examples/mage/data
IN=(--geno-list $D/geno/mage.pgen_list.tsv
    --pheno $D/pheno/mage_expr.chr21_22.regenie.tsv.gz
    --trait-annot $D/pheno/mage_genes.chr21_22.bed
    --pairs $D/reference/gtex_lcl_eqtl.chr21_22.tsv.gz)
COV=(--cov $D/pheno/mage_covariates.regenie.tsv.gz)

anqchor trans run "${IN[@]}"                                              --out results/trans/nocov
anqchor trans run "${IN[@]}" "${COV[@]}" --cov-include sex,PC1-5          --out results/trans/basic
anqchor trans run "${IN[@]}" "${COV[@]}" --cov-include sex,PC1-5,PEER1-10 --out results/trans/peer10
anqchor trans run "${IN[@]}" "${COV[@]}"                                  --out results/trans/peer60
anqchor trans run "${IN[@]}" "${COV[@]}" --rint                           --out results/trans/peer60_rint

(IN and COV are shell arrays, so the commands work in both bash and zsh.)

Setup Covariates Phenotypes nocov none (no --cov) as given basic sex and 5 genotype PCs (ancestry) as given peer10 + 10 PEER factors (hidden expression factors) as given peer60 all 66 (every column of --cov) as given peer60_rint all 66 rank-based inverse normal transform after covariate adjustment (--rint)

Each run prints its steps and stops at the summary tables (no HTML). The peer10 run, for example, prints (running it a second time prints ran: nothing (all steps up to date)):

$ anqchor trans run "${IN[@]}" "${COV[@]}" --cov-include sex,PC1-5,PEER1-10 --out results/trans/peer10
[anqchor] running prepare.genotypes
[anqchor] running prepare.reference.reference
[anqchor] running prepare.dataset.dataset
[anqchor] running prepare.mapping.dataset.reference
[anqchor] running trans.dataset.lists
[anqchor] running trans.dataset.default.inputs
[anqchor] running trans.dataset.default.rect.raw
[anqchor] running trans.dataset.summarize
ran: prepare.genotypes, prepare.reference.reference, ..., trans.dataset.summarize

Runtime: about 8 seconds per run on a laptop. The runs are independent, so you can start them at the same time: in five terminals, as five cluster jobs, or in one shell by ending each command with & and then typing wait. With flags only, the dataset is called dataset, the reference reference and the covariate set default; the run directory name says which setup it is. Running the same command again does nothing (ran: nothing (all steps up to date)).

docs.title: Compare the runs
docs.text:
anqchor trans compare results/trans/nocov results/trans/basic results/trans/peer10 \
    results/trans/peer60 results/trans/peer60_rint --out results/trans/compare

warning: nocov: p-values inflated (λGC 1.74 across chromosomes, above 1.1)
compared 5 run(s): nocov, basic, peer10, peer60, peer60_rint
tables: results/trans/compare
trans report: results/trans/compare/report/trans.html

This takes about 1 second and runs no association test. Each run is labelled with its directory name; give --label once per run, in order, to choose other labels. --out must be a new directory or an earlier trans comparison, which is then replaced. The warning is the nocov run's own: its cross-chromosome tests are inflated (see below). anqchor also checks that the runs are comparable, the same genotype and phenotype samples, reference, rectangle, cell counts and opening hotspot setting, and warns about any difference; here there is none, so every number on the page is over the same 126,982 cells.

--no-report writes the tables only. To re-render the HTML later (for example after updating anqchor), run

anqchor trans report --out results/trans/compare

trans report: results/trans/compare/report/trans.html

which reads the comparison's tables and rewrites report/trans.html in about 1 second. anqchor trans report --out results/trans/peer10 renders the page of a single run in the same way.

docs.title: What comes out
docs.text:
Each run:

results/trans/peer10/
├── trans/dataset/
│   ├── summary.json            the run's numbers: cells, replication, hotspot grid, inflation
│   ├── reference_pairs.tsv     every reference pair: class, effect, −log10 p, replicated or not
│   ├── hotspots.tsv            every 1-Mb bin: genes with a trans signal per threshold
│   ├── hotspot_genes.tsv       every bin and gene with a trans signal at p < 1e-4
│   ├── qq.tsv                  QQ points of the cross-chromosome cells, with the 95% band
│   ├── variants.tsv            per variant: cells by class, trans signals, strongest genes
│   ├── pairs.sig.tsv.gz        every cell with p < 1e-5
│   └── strategies/default/     cov.regenie.tsv.gz, strategy.json, rect_assoc.raw.tsv.gz
├── anqchor.resolved.yaml       all settings, flags included
└── run.json                    provenance

The comparison:

results/trans/compare/
├── runs.tsv                one row per run: inputs, cells, replication, λ_GC, observed counts, hotspots
├── hotspot_grid.tsv        hotspots per run, threshold and minimum genes
├── hotspots.tsv            the runs' bins (column run)

├── settings/<run>.anqchor.yaml   each run's complete settings
